newsitem.title: CROATIA: FEATURE - Croatia gets foot in EU door but entry a long way off.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Croatia gets foot in EU door but entry a long way off.

text.p: "At last," many Croatians murmured when their young country was ushered this month into the Council of Europe, foyer of the European Union, after four years of waiting.

But Croatia, which had fumed in the queue while other states with less than perfect credentials jumped ahead into the Council, has a long, hard road ahead to acceptance by the privileged club of democracies.
Authoritarian nationalists still dominate Croatia and EU arbiters will be looking for new, post-war trends towards democracy and tolerance to take root before closer links are offered to Zagreb.

The Council of Europe decided on October 16 to admit Croatia as its 40th member state, binding the ex-Yugoslav republic to EU convenants on democracy and human rights while opening the door to EU aid and trade schemes.

Croatia clamoured to join EU institutions in the early 1990s like other East European states shedding communist rule at the time. But it had a handicap -- involvement in the wars of the Yugoslav succession.

Western analysts say the EU was alienated by Croatia's bid to grab land in Bosnia, mirroring a pre-1945 "Greater Croatia", and also by its war at home with minority Serbs who resisted its 1991 secession from federal Yugoslavia.
Croatia had to change course to rehabilitate its application for Council membership, the ticket to Western aid needed to help restructure and privatise its war-shattered economy.
Croats have historically gravitated towards the West, with many having emigrated since 1900 in search of economic opportunity and political freedom.
In the past year Zagreb has wooed Western favour by:
-- Co-signing the 1995 Dayton peace treaty brokered by the United States to preserve Bosnia as one state.
-- Accepting a United Nations-supervised handover of the last Serb enclave in Croatia after retaking two others by force, displacing 150,000 Serbs in an orgy of looting and burning.
-- Signing a diplomatic normalisation treaty with rump Yugoslavia, whose main republic is Serbia.
-- Ensuring Bosnian Croats cooperated with post-war unity elections in Bosnia, held peacefully in September.
-- Broadening a war amnesty for Croatian Serbs.
-- Passing legislation to define press freedoms.

"Croatia's image was controversial for some time. Now we feel it has left its phase of military confrontation behind and can look forward to normalisation not just with others, but within its own society," said a senior European diplomat.

But Western political analysts say Croatia is not yet a fully-fledged democracy because the interests of the ruling party still tend to outweigh the rule of law when naked power and prickly national pride are at stake.
Independent Croatia's constitution is unequivocally democratic. But key laws have not been consistently enforced, above all in areas of minority rights and freedom of speech.

"We must see further advances on democracy issues before Croatia moves closer to the EU with an association agreement, perhaps in a year's time if Eastern Slavonia (Serb enclave) is resolved peacefully," said another European diplomat.

Of deepest concern for the EU is Croatia's failure to extradite Croats indicted by the U.N. tribunal on war crimes in former Yugoslavia, even though parliament has enacted a law on cooperation with the international court.
Another problem is President Franjo Tudjman's refusal to recognise an opposition coalition victory over his HDZ party in elections for the Zagreb regional government a year ago.

The HDZ cites "national security" concerns and claims its rivals, now boycotting city council in protest at HDZ nominees administering the city, are too divided and feckless to govern either locally or nationally.
"A government cannot choose to ignore electoral defeat if it aims to enter the EU," a diplomat said. "Basic standards of democracy are an indivisible part of the process."

The EU also disapproves of the government's intolerance of independent media who criticise Tudjman's autocratic style and have exposed apparent profiteering from Croatia's privatisation programme by HDZ-linked figures.

The government has used state television (HRT), the main source of news for Croats, to promote the HDZ and pillory foes. It has silenced critical newspapers by forced buyouts and tried to gag others with punitive taxes and lawsuits.
But winds of democratic change have started to blow.
Two journalists charged with slandering Tudjman, a former communist general, were acquitted by a state court last month.
Now there are moves to form an independent television network led by former HRT journalists fed up with censorship.

Democratic currents are also noticeable in a swing of voters, especially younger educated people, away from the HDZ towards moderate, civic parties ahead of countrywide communal and presidential elections in 1997.

Polls show that, with the war over, Croats no longer see a need for indefinite, unconditional HDZ rule and complain of HDZ insensitivity to a war-induced fall in living standards while a favoured few get fat from fraudulent privatisation.
"What the EU expects from Croatia now is a thorough reform of its political and economic (culture)," said Davor Gjenero, an independent Croatian commentator.
European diplomats say Croatia could set its sights on EU membership sometime after 2000 if it embraces democracy.
